All at once deployment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Immutable deployments launch new instances in a temporary group, keeping full capacity and allowing quick rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• In-place single batch: In-place updates reduce capacity and are harder to roll back.
• Rolling without batches: Rolling reduces capacity during updates.
• All at once deployment: All at once causes downtime.

Key takeaway: Full capacity and easy rollback → immutable deployments.

stem: A team wants to trigger an automated fix whenever an EBS volume is created without encryption. Which combination fits?

choices.text: An EventBridge rule or Config rule that invokes an SSM Automation runbook
A monthly CSV export of volumes reviewed by the security team
A Route 53 health check on the EC2 instance using the volume
A CloudFront distribution that caches the current volume list for the operations users

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Event- or Config-based detection that triggers Automation runbooks enables automated remediation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A monthly CSV export of volumes reviewed by…: Monthly reviews are slow and manual.
• A Route 53 health check on the EC2 instance…: Health checks do not inspect volumes.
• A CloudFront distribution that caches the…: CloudFront is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Detect and remediate with events and Automation runbooks.

stem: A company wants to run scheduled maintenance tasks, such as Run Command documents, on groups of instances only during approved hours. Which feature fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs retention settings
AWS Config aggregator schedules
EC2 Instance Scheduler on Lambda only
Systems Manager Maintenance Windows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Maintenance Windows define schedules and targets for running tasks such as Run Command and Automation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch Logs retention settings: Retention settings manage logs.
• AWS Config aggregator schedules: Aggregators collect Config data.
• EC2 Instance Scheduler on Lambda only: Instance scheduling starts and stops instances but is not a task window.

Key takeaway: Schedule operational tasks with Maintenance Windows.

stem: EC2 instances are not appearing as managed instances in Systems Manager. Which TWO items should be checked? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The instances have Elastic IP addresses associated
The instance profile includes the required SSM permissions
The instances have termination protection enabled
The instances use the largest available instance type
The SSM Agent is installed and running on the instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed instances need a running SSM Agent, permissions (such as AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore), and network access to SSM endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The instances have Elastic IP addresses…: Elastic IPs are not required.
• The instances have termination protection…: Termination protection is irrelevant.
• The instances use the largest available…: Instance size is irrelevant.

Key takeaway: SSM management needs the agent, permissions, and connectivity.

stem: A private subnet with no internet access hosts instances that must be managed by Systems Manager. What is required?

choices.text: An internet gateway attached to the private subnet's route table
A public IP address assigned to each instance at launch
Interface VPC endpoints for SSM, SSM messages, and EC2 messages
A VPC peering connection to a public subnet in another VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Without internet access, instances reach Systems Manager through interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An internet gateway attached to the private…: That would make the subnet public.
• A public IP address assigned to each…: Public IPs require internet routing.
• A VPC peering connection to a public subnet…: Peering does not provide access to AWS service endpoints.

Key takeaway: Private SSM access → interface endpoints.

stem: A team wants to update the AMI used by an Auto Scaling group and gradually replace running instances. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Termination protection on every existing instance
Instance refresh with the updated launch template
Detaching all instances and launching them manually
A scheduled scaling action to zero at midnight

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Instance refresh replaces instances in batches according to minimum healthy percentage, using the new launch template.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Termination protection on every existing…: Termination protection blocks replacement.
• Detaching all instances and launching them…: Manual replacement is error-prone.
• A scheduled scaling action to zero at midnight: Scaling to zero causes an outage.

Key takeaway: Roll out new AMIs with instance refresh.

stem: A team must create identical test environments frequently and tear them down after use. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Define the environment in CloudFormation and create or delete stacks
Keep one permanent test environment that everyone shares forever
Copy production data and servers manually for each test cycle
Build each environment manually in the console and delete by hand

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Infrastructure as code creates repeatable environments and deletes all resources together.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keep one permanent test environment that…: A shared permanent environment causes conflicts.
• Copy production data and servers manually…: Manual copying is error-prone.
• Build each environment manually in the…: Manual builds are slow and inconsistent.

Key takeaway: Repeatable environments come from IaC.

stem: A company needs to share an AMI with another AWS account securely. The AMI uses encrypted EBS snapshots. What must also be shared?

choices.text: The root user password of the source account that owns the AMI
The CloudTrail trail of the source account
Access to the KMS key used to encrypt the snapshots
The VPC and subnets where the AMI was built

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Encrypted AMIs require the target account to have permission to use the KMS key (a customer managed key).

Why the other options are wrong:
• The root user password of the source account…: Root passwords must never be shared.
• The CloudTrail trail of the source account: CloudTrail is unrelated.
• The VPC and subnets where the AMI was built: Networks are not needed to share AMIs.

Key takeaway: Sharing encrypted AMIs requires KMS key access.

stem: A company deploys containers and wants AWS to manage the servers entirely while it defines only tasks and services. Which option fits?

choices.text: Amazon ECS on self-managed EC2
Kubernetes on on-premises VMs
Docker on a single EC2 host
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fargate runs containers without managing servers or clusters of instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon ECS on self-managed EC2: EC2 launch type requires managing instances.
• Kubernetes on on-premises VMs: On-premises VMs require full management.
• Docker on a single EC2 host: A single host must be managed and is a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: Serverless containers → Fargate.

stem: A team wants every S3 bucket created in the account to have default encryption and tags, enforced automatically. Which TWO mechanisms help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: CloudFormation templates or Service Catalog products used for bucket creation
Disabling CloudTrail so creations are not logged
A dashboard listing bucket names by creation date
A weekly email reminding engineers to add tags
AWS Config rules with automatic remediation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Standardized templates build compliant buckets, and Config rules catch and fix buckets created outside them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling CloudTrail so creations are not logged: Disabling logs removes auditing.
• A dashboard listing bucket names by creation…: Dashboards do not enforce settings.
• A weekly email reminding engineers to add tags: Reminders are not enforcement.

Key takeaway: Enforce standards with templates plus detective remediation.

stem: A CloudFormation stack deletion fails because an S3 bucket in the stack still contains objects. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Add a new tag to the bucket and try the deletion one more time
Delete the AWS account that owns the stack and the bucket
Change the bucket's storage class to S3 Glacier Deep Archive
Empty the bucket, or retain it, and then retry the deletion

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation cannot delete non-empty buckets; emptying them (or retaining them) allows deletion to proceed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Add a new tag to the bucket and try the…: Tags do not remove objects.
• Delete the AWS account that owns the stack…: Deleting the account is drastic.
• Change the bucket's storage class to S3…: Storage class does not affect deletion.

Key takeaway: Empty or retain S3 buckets before deleting stacks.

stem: A company wants configuration changes to Lambda-based operational scripts to go through code review and automatic deployment. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Email code changes to an administrator who pastes them into Lambda
Store the code in a repository with a CodePipeline that deploys on merge
Keep scripts only on one engineer's laptop and upload them manually
Edit functions directly in the console during production incidents

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A version-controlled repository with an automated pipeline provides review, traceability, and consistent deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Email code changes to an administrator who…: Emailing code is error-prone.
• Keep scripts only on one engineer's laptop…: Laptop-only scripts are fragile and unreviewed.
• Edit functions directly in the console…: Console edits bypass review.

Key takeaway: Manage operational code through version control and pipelines.

stem: A team needs to provision the same resources in multiple Regions from one CloudFormation template, with Region-specific values such as instance types. Which template feature fits?

choices.text: Stack policies that deny all updates to resources
DependsOn attributes between all resources
Mappings keyed by Region with Fn::FindInMap
Outputs exported under the same name everywhere

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Mappings provide lookup tables, such as Region-specific values, retrieved with Fn::FindInMap.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stack policies that deny all updates to…: Stack policies protect resources.
• DependsOn attributes between all resources: DependsOn controls order.
• Outputs exported under the same name everywhere: Outputs expose values; export names must be unique per Region.

Key takeaway: Region-specific values → Mappings and FindInMap.

stem: A company wants to patch only instances tagged Environment=Dev first, then Prod a week later. Which Patch Manager approach fits?

choices.text: Disabling patching for Prod entirely to avoid any application risk
One maintenance window that patches every instance in all accounts and environments at once
Manual patching of each instance by logging in over SSH each week
Separate patch groups or targets by tag with different maintenance windows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Targeting by tags with separate windows lets teams stage patching from Dev to Prod.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling patching for Prod entirely to…: Skipping Prod patches leaves vulnerabilities.
• One maintenance window that patches every…: Patching everything at once removes staging.
• Manual patching of each instance by logging…: Manual patching does not scale.

Key takeaway: Stage patching with tag-based targets and windows.

stem: A company wants to test how its application behaves when an Availability Zone becomes unavailable, in a controlled way. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Fault Injection Service
AWS Trusted Advisor checks
AWS Compute Optimizer
Amazon Inspector

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fault Injection Service runs controlled experiments, such as AZ disruptions, to test resilience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Trusted Advisor checks: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.
• AWS Compute Optimizer: Compute Optimizer recommends sizes.
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector finds vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: Test resilience with Fault Injection Service.

stem: A company wants a single sign-on experience for employees accessing multiple AWS accounts with centrally managed permissions. Which service fits?

choices.text: IAM users in every account
Amazon Cognito user pools
AWS IAM Identity Center
AWS Directory Service only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center provides SSO across accounts with permission sets assigned centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM users in every account: Per-account IAM users do not provide SSO and are hard to manage.
• Amazon Cognito user pools: Cognito targets customer-facing application users.
• AWS Directory Service only: Directory Service alone does not assign AWS account permissions.

Key takeaway: Workforce SSO across accounts → IAM Identity Center.

stem: An application on EC2 needs to read from a DynamoDB table. What is the most secure way to give it credentials?

choices.text: Access keys stored in the application's config file
An IAM role attached through an instance profile
The root user's access keys set as environment variables
A shared IAM user's password hard-coded into the code

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Instance profiles deliver temporary, automatically rotated credentials from an IAM role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access keys stored in the application's…: Stored long-term keys can leak.
• The root user's access keys set as…: Root keys must never be used this way.
• A shared IAM user's password hard-coded into…: Hard-coded passwords are insecure.

Key takeaway: Give EC2 access through IAM roles, not stored keys.

stem: A security team wants all API activity from every account in the organization recorded to one central bucket. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: A separate trail in only the management account
An organization trail in AWS CloudTrail
VPC Flow Logs for every VPC in the organization
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries in each account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An organization trail logs events for all member accounts to a central location.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A separate trail in only the management account: A management-account trail alone does not cover members unless it is an organization trail.
• VPC Flow Logs for every VPC in the organization: Flow Logs capture network traffic, not API calls.
• CloudWatch Logs Insights queries in each account: Queries do not record events.

Key takeaway: Organization-wide API logging → organization trail.

stem: Security must detect and alert whenever the root user signs in to any account. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A CloudWatch dashboard showing the number of IAM users per account
A monthly review of IAM credential reports by the security team
An EventBridge rule on root sign-in events from CloudTrail with an SNS target
An AWS Config rule that checks S3 bucket encryption settings daily

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail records console sign-in events; an EventBridge rule can match root sign-ins and notify through SNS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A CloudWatch dashboard showing the number of…: User counts do not detect sign-ins.
• A monthly review of IAM credential reports…: Monthly reviews are too slow.
• An AWS Config rule that checks S3 bucket…: Encryption checks are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Alert on root sign-ins with CloudTrail events and EventBridge.

stem: A company must encrypt data in an S3 bucket with keys it controls and audit every key use. Which option fits?

choices.text: No encryption with bucket versioning
SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys
Client-side encryption with no key logs
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key gives control over key policies and logs key usage in CloudTrail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No encryption with bucket versioning: Versioning is not encryption.
• SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3 without customer control.
• Client-side encryption with no key logs: No logging fails the audit requirement.

Key takeaway: Controlled, auditable S3 encryption → SSE-KMS with a CMK.

stem: A company wants to protect its public web application from large DDoS attacks, with access to the AWS response team and cost protection. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Shield Advanced
AWS Shield Standard
Network ACLs only
Security groups only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds enhanced DDoS protection, access to the Shield Response Team, and cost protection for scaling during attacks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Shield Standard: Shield Standard provides baseline protection without those features.
• Network ACLs only: NACLs cannot absorb large DDoS attacks.
• Security groups only: Security groups do not stop DDoS attacks.

Key takeaway: Enhanced DDoS protection and support → Shield Advanced.

stem: A company needs TLS certificates for its ALBs that renew automatically. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Secrets Manager rotating certificate text
AWS Certificate Manager public certificates
Certificates stored in an S3 bucket manually
Self-signed certificates on each EC2 instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ACM issues and automatically renews public certificates for integrated services such as ALB.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Secrets Manager rotating certificate text: Secrets Manager stores secrets but does not issue public certificates.
• Certificates stored in an S3 bucket manually: Manual storage lacks renewal.
• Self-signed certificates on each EC2 instance: Self-signed certificates are not trusted by browsers.

Key takeaway: Auto-renewing certificates for ALBs → ACM.

stem: Which TWO controls help protect EC2 instances in a web tier? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Public IPs and open SSH from anywhere on every instance
Disabling OS patching to avoid application changes
Security groups allowing only required ports from the ALB
Shared access keys stored on each instance's disk
Private subnets for instances behind the load balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Least-privilege security groups and private placement behind the ALB reduce the attack surface.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IPs and open SSH from anywhere on…: Open SSH exposes instances.
• Disabling OS patching to avoid application…: Unpatched systems are vulnerable.
• Shared access keys stored on each instance's…: Stored shared keys can leak.

Key takeaway: Limit exposure with tight security groups and private subnets.

stem: A company must keep AWS Config recording enabled in every account and Region of its organization. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Deploy Config with StackSets and deny StopConfigurationRecorder with an SCP
Ask each account owner to check Config settings once per year
Enable Config only in the management account's home Region
Store Config data in a public S3 bucket for easy access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
StackSets deploy Config everywhere, and an SCP prevents member accounts from stopping the recorder.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ask each account owner to check Config…: Annual checks are not enforcement.
• Enable Config only in the management…: One account and Region is insufficient.
• Store Config data in a public S3 bucket for…: Public buckets expose data.

Key takeaway: Deploy widely with StackSets and lock with SCPs.

stem: An auditor needs evidence that KMS keys used for production data are rotated. What should the operations team enable?

choices.text: Manual key deletion every 30 days for all keys
Disabling CloudTrail logging for KMS API calls
Key sharing with all accounts in the organization
Automatic key rotation for the customer managed keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automatic rotation for customer managed keys generates new key material on a schedule, and rotation status can be shown to auditors.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual key deletion every 30 days for all keys: Deleting keys makes encrypted data unreadable.
• Disabling CloudTrail logging for KMS API calls: Disabling logs removes evidence.
• Key sharing with all accounts in the…: Sharing keys widely increases risk.

Key takeaway: Enable automatic rotation for customer managed KMS keys.

stem: A team wants to investigate the root cause of a GuardDuty finding by analyzing related activity over time. Which service helps?

choices.text: Amazon Detective
AWS DataSync
Amazon Polly
Amazon Lightsail

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Detective organizes log data into graphs that help investigate security findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS DataSync: DataSync transfers data.
• Amazon Polly: Polly synthesizes speech.
• Amazon Lightsail: Lightsail hosts simple applications.

Key takeaway: Investigate findings with Amazon Detective.

stem: A company wants to manage WAF rules and Shield protections consistently across all accounts in its organization. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Resource Groups
AWS Firewall Manager
AWS Cloud Map
AWS Health Dashboard

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Firewall Manager centrally configures WAF, Shield Advanced, security groups, and Network Firewall across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Resource Groups: Resource Groups organize resources.
• AWS Cloud Map: Cloud Map handles service discovery.
• AWS Health Dashboard: The Health Dashboard shows service events.

Key takeaway: Central firewall policy across accounts → Firewall Manager.

stem: Which TWO practices strengthen IAM security for human users? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Keep unused access keys active forever
Share one admin user among the team
Require MFA for console sign-in
Grant AdministratorAccess to every user
Use temporary credentials through roles

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MFA protects sign-ins, and temporary credentials via roles avoid long-lived keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keep unused access keys active forever: Unused keys increase risk.
• Share one admin user among the team: Shared users remove accountability.
• Grant AdministratorAccess to every user: Broad permissions violate least privilege.

Key takeaway: Use MFA and temporary credentials.

stem: A company needs a dedicated, consistent-bandwidth private connection from its data center to AWS. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront
AWS Client VPN
AWS Site-to-Site VPN
AWS Direct Connect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity with consistent performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront is a CDN.
• AWS Client VPN: Client VPN connects individual users.
• AWS Site-to-Site VPN: VPN runs over the internet with variable performance.

Key takeaway: Dedicated, consistent private link → Direct Connect.

stem: A Direct Connect link must have a backup path if it fails, at low cost. Which option fits?

choices.text: A CloudFront distribution in front of the VPC
A second VPC with no hybrid connectivity
An internet gateway on the on-premises side
A Site-to-Site VPN as a backup connection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A VPN over the internet is a common low-cost backup for Direct Connect.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A CloudFront distribution in front of the VPC: CloudFront does not provide hybrid connectivity.
• A second VPC with no hybrid connectivity: Another VPC does not connect on-premises.
• An internet gateway on the on-premises side: Internet gateways are AWS VPC components.

Key takeaway: Back up Direct Connect with a Site-to-Site VPN.

stem: Remote employees need secure access to resources in a VPC from their laptops. Which service fits?

choices.text: VPC peering links
AWS Direct Connect
AWS Client VPN
NAT gateways only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Client VPN provides managed remote-access VPN for users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering links: Peering connects VPCs.
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect links data centers, not individual laptops.
• NAT gateways only: NAT gateways provide outbound internet access.

Key takeaway: Remote user access to VPCs → Client VPN.

stem: A company wants to split traffic 90/10 between the current and new versions of its application using DNS. Which Route 53 policy fits?

choices.text: Weighted routing
Failover routing
Geolocation routing
Latency routing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing distributes traffic by assigned weights.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Failover routing: Failover routes by health.
• Geolocation routing: Geolocation routes by location.
• Latency routing: Latency routing uses network latency.

Key takeaway: Percentage-based DNS traffic split → weighted routing.

stem: A CloudFront distribution must serve personalized API responses and cached static assets from the same domain. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: One cache behavior with a 24-hour TTL for every request
Separate cache behaviors by path with different caching settings
Disable caching for the entire distribution's traffic
Use a separate distribution per user for personalization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Path-based cache behaviors let static paths be cached while API paths bypass or minimize caching.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One cache behavior with a 24-hour TTL for…: Caching personalized responses for 24 hours is incorrect.
• Disable caching for the entire…: Disabling caching loses static benefits.
• Use a separate distribution per user for…: A distribution per user is impractical.

Key takeaway: Use path-based cache behaviors for mixed content.

stem: Instances in a private subnet cannot reach the internet. A NAT gateway exists. Which TWO items should be checked? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The instances use an encrypted EBS root volume
The private route table has 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway
The VPC has a private hosted zone in Route 53
The instances have Elastic IP addresses attached
The NAT gateway is in a public subnet with an IGW route

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private subnets need a default route to the NAT gateway, and the NAT gateway must sit in a public subnet with an internet gateway route.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The instances use an encrypted EBS root volume: Volume encryption is unrelated.
• The VPC has a private hosted zone in Route 53: Private hosted zones are for DNS.
• The instances have Elastic IP addresses attached: Private instances do not need Elastic IPs.

Key takeaway: Check both route tables for NAT-based internet access.

stem: On-premises servers cannot resolve names in a Route 53 private hosted zone over Direct Connect. What should be configured?

choices.text: A public hosted zone copy of every private record for the servers
A CloudFront distribution in front of the private hosted zone
A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint with on-premises DNS forwarding
A NAT gateway in the VPC for on-premises DNS queries to use

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resolver inbound endpoints let on-premises DNS servers forward queries to resolve private hosted zone names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A public hosted zone copy of every private…: Copying to public zones exposes internal records.
• A CloudFront distribution in front of the…: CloudFront does not serve DNS.
• A NAT gateway in the VPC for on-premises DNS…: NAT gateways do not resolve DNS.

Key takeaway: On-premises resolution of private zones → Resolver inbound endpoint.

stem: Users receive 502 errors from an ALB. Targets show as healthy, but the application sometimes closes connections unexpectedly. What is a likely cause?

choices.text: The target's keep-alive timeout is shorter than the ALB idle timeout
The target group uses more than one Availability Zone for targets
The Route 53 alias record for the ALB uses a TTL that is too short
The ALB's access logs bucket has versioning enabled on its objects

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the target closes idle connections before the ALB does, the ALB may reuse a closed connection and return 502.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The target group uses more than one…: Multiple AZs are normal.
• The Route 53 alias record for the ALB uses a…: DNS TTL does not cause 502s.
• The ALB's access logs bucket has versioning…: Log bucket settings are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Set target keep-alive longer than the ALB idle timeout.

stem: A company needs to block access to its CloudFront content from specific countries. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Route 53 latency-based routing
S3 bucket versioning settings
EC2 security group outbound rules
CloudFront geographic restrictions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront geographic restrictions allow or block viewers by country.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 latency-based routing: Latency routing directs traffic, not blocks.
• S3 bucket versioning settings: Versioning keeps object versions.
• EC2 security group outbound rules: Security groups do not apply to CloudFront viewers.

Key takeaway: Block countries at the edge with geo restrictions.

stem: A team wants to apply the same set of tags automatically to all resources created by a CloudFormation stack. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm for resources that have no tags
Add tags manually in each service console after deployment
Specify stack-level tags when creating or updating the stack
Use an S3 lifecycle rule to add tags to resources nightly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Stack-level tags propagate to supported resources created by the stack.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Create a CloudWatch alarm for resources that…: Alarms do not apply tags.
• Add tags manually in each service console…: Manual tagging is error-prone.
• Use an S3 lifecycle rule to add tags to…: Lifecycle rules do not tag resources.

Key takeaway: Propagate tags with stack-level tags.
